Below is a synthesis of what recent wage-gap review papers recommend for future systematic reviews, followed by which recommendation is most strongly justified by the evidence gaps they themselves identify.

# What review papers identify as high-priority topics for future systematic reviews

- Causal identification and quasi-experimental designs
  - Reviewers consistently call for studies that move beyond correlation to identify causal mechanisms behind pay gaps, emphasizing quasi-experiments, instrumental variables, and policy natural experiments to attribute effects to gendered practices, discrimination, or structural barriers rather than confounded differences in human capital or choice. <cite id="cdcb9664-2">With the exception of the European Union, no jurisdiction has contemplated the need for the sort of rigorous research that is necessary to sustain public support and ethical justification for pay equity policies; with the onus on advocates to show these policies do more good than harm, rigorous, causal analyses are highlighted as a gap and a priority for future research agendas. 
  - Reviews of interventions also urge systematic synthesis on the effectiveness and side effects of institutional remedies (e.g., bans on salary history questions, pay transparency) to clarify causal links between policy changes and pay equity outcomes. <cite id="99f6604d-0">A review of interventions to reduce gender gaps in negotiation outcomes assesses effectiveness in reducing the gender pay gap and flags unintended consequences that warrant caution, underscoring the need for more causal and policy-focused evaluations.</cite>

- Intersectionality and heterogeneity across identities and work arrangements
  - Meta-reviews and policy evidence syntheses stress that the “gender pay gap” masks large within-country heterogeneity across race/ethnicity, disability, part-time/contract work, sector, occupation, firm size, and institutional context. <cite id="cdcb9664-1">Comparative literature highlights that differences in industrial and occupational segregation, returns to characteristics, and national wage structures account for substantial cross-country variation; within countries, the residual gap often reflects unobserved structural and institutional conditions, motivating systematic analyses that stratify by identity and work arrangements.</cite> 
  - Reviews in related domains show that gender-blind research practices and poor reporting on sex/gender contribute to persistent evidence gaps on equity impacts, reinforcing the need for intersectional, disaggregated future syntheses. <cite id="50ae3102-1">A reanalysis finds that gendered impact assessments are substantially less common than cost-effectiveness analyses and documents inadequate reporting of sex/gender across methods and results, suggesting that intersectional, disaggregated reviews are needed to close these gaps.</cite>

- Measurement and definitions (wages vs earnings; job-to-job vs tenure; within vs between firm; overtime/commissions)
  - Evidence reviews repeatedly note that widely used statistics (e.g., gender pay gap ratios) vary in definitions and denominators (average hourly wages vs median income; full-time vs all workers), and that pay components such as overtime and commissions are inconsistently measured. <cite id="fbc200a3-1">Global monitoring bodies report global gender pay gaps using average hourly wages for 73 countries (16%), with alternative factor-weighted estimates (19%), while OECD data show median income gaps of about 13.5% with wide cross-country variation; these discrepancies by metric and coverage motivate standardized measurement protocols in future reviews.</cite>
  - Reviews of decomposition techniques and sectoral comparisons emphasize the need for consistent decomposition frameworks and clearer attribution of “within-firm” versus “between-firm/sectoral” drivers across institutional contexts. <cite id="cdcb9664-0">Decomposition-based reviews attribute inter-sector gender pay gap dynamics to national wage structures and cross-country differences in returns to characteristics, underscoring the need for standardized decomposition and measurement practices in future syntheses.</cite>

- Sectoral/occupational segregation and occupational mobility
  - Cross-country reviews highlight that segregation patterns and national wage structures shape observed gender pay gaps, calling for systematic comparisons of sectoral/occupational segregation, occupational mobility, and returns across institutions. <cite id="cdcb9664-1">Cross-country studies identify national wage structures and cross-country differences in industrial and occupational segregation and returns to these characteristics as determinants of the GPG, suggesting a need for systematic, comparative analyses of segregation and mobility.</cite>
  - Policy-oriented reviews recommend mapping segregation dynamics over time to link segregation to pay gap trajectories and to evaluate impacts of sector-specific policies. <cite id="fbc200a3-2">ILO’s initiative on the wage gap between men and women in Latin America brings 173 countries together to address SDG Target 8.5, reflecting a regional agenda to systematically analyze sectoral and institutional drivers; this implies prioritizing sectoral/occupational breakdowns and cross-jurisdictional comparisons in future reviews.</cite>

- Data systems, transparency, and gender-blindness in research infrastructure
  - Reviews diagnose that many studies are gender-blind by design, with inconsistent reporting of sex/gender across methods and results and inadequate terminology (sex vs gender), which obscures equity-relevant heterogeneity. <cite id="50ae3102-1">Meta-analyses show that while sex/gender is often mentioned in methods (51–83%), it is reported in results less than 30% of the time, and terminology is inconsistently used; these gaps justify recommendations for standardized, gender-aware data collection, reporting, and registries for future systematic reviews.</cite>
  - Policy evidence syntheses argue that jurisdictions lack rigorous, jurisdiction-specific impact evaluations of pay equity policies, pointing to the need for centralized, comparable administrative data and transparency regimes to support systematic synthesis. <cite id="cdcb9664-2">No jurisdiction appears to contemplate the need for rigorous research to sustain pay equity policies’ ethical justification; future research agendas should include building comparable data systems and transparent evaluation protocols.</cite>

- Mechanism-focused and expectation-driven research
  - Survey reviews of beliefs and expectations emphasize under-studied mechanisms (e.g., biased beliefs, negotiation styles) and call for systematic tests of how these mechanisms interact with human capital and institutional context. <cite id="99f6604d-2">Evidence shows a U-shaped gender pay gap across the wage distribution and documents gender gaps in expected starting and lifetime earnings; related studies attribute substantial gaps to sorting and negotiation styles, motivating future mechanism-focused syntheses on beliefs, negotiation, and career pathing.</cite>
  - Reviews of negotiation interventions urge standardized evaluation designs and attention to unintended consequences, pointing to the need for systematic reviews that combine lab/field evidence with administrative outcomes. <cite id="99f6604d-0">A review of negotiation interventions and institutional changes documents both promise and unintended consequences, recommending standardized, causal evaluation frameworks and transparent reporting in future systematic reviews.</cite>

- Global and regional coverage with attention to non-OECD and emerging-economy contexts
  - Cross-national reviews note that progress differs sharply across OECD vs non-OECD countries and across EU member states, calling for systematic reviews that expand geographic coverage and harmonize measurement. <cite id="fbc200a3-1">According to OECD data, the differential in median income is about 13.5% and improving in OECD countries, while for non-OECD countries it is around 15% and worsening; across the EU, the salary gap ranges from 1.3% (Luxembourg) to 22.3% (Latvia), indicating a strong need for systematic, geographically disaggregated evidence syntheses.</cite>

# How the cited evidence gaps motivate these recommendations

- Why causal identification: reviews highlight that policy debates demand ex ante/ex post justifications and that rigorous causal research is underdeveloped relative to descriptive assessments, with pay equity policies often justified by positive claims alone. <cite id="cdcb9664-2">The policy analytic approach reveals that pay equity policies struggle to meet standard criteria of justification; rigorous causal research has been uncommon, and the onus is on advocates to demonstrate benefits exceed harms, underscoring the need for causal designs and systematic policy evaluations.</cite>

- Why intersectionality and heterogeneity: decomposition and cross-country comparisons show that unexplained residuals reflect institutional structures (wage structures, segregation, returns), not just individual differences, motivating disaggregated, intersectional analyses and standardized reporting. <cite id="cdcb9664-1">Observed gaps persist after accounting for observable characteristics, and differences in wage structures, segregation, and returns across countries and institutions explain much of the variation, implying that future reviews must stratify by identity, sector, and occupation with consistent measurement.</cite> <cite id="50ae3102-1">Gender-blind reporting and terminology inconsistencies leave key equity dimensions under-studied, justifying intersectional, disaggregated future syntheses.</cite>

- Why measurement standardization: conflicting definitions and coverage yield widely varying gap magnitudes; reviews note the need for consistent metrics (wages vs earnings; job-to-job vs tenure; within vs between firm) and pay components. <cite id="fbc200a3-1">Global monitoring uses different bases (average hourly wages vs median income) and shows large cross-country variation; this motivates standardized, comparable metrics in future systematic reviews.</cite> <cite id="cdcb9664-0">Decomposition methods attribute sectoral differences to national wage structures and returns, reinforcing a need for transparent, comparable decomposition protocols.</cite>

- Why sectoral/occupational segregation: cross-country analyses attribute substantial gaps to segregation and institutional context, calling for systematic comparisons and policy-linked evaluations. <cite id="cdcb9664-1">National wage structures and segregation patterns drive gap magnitude; systematic reviews should compare these mechanisms across institutions and over time.</cite> <cite id="fbc200a3-2">International initiatives to monitor wage gaps imply a research agenda emphasizing sectoral/occupational breakdowns and cross-jurisdictional comparisons.</cite>

- Why data/registry and transparency: pervasive gender-blindness and inconsistent reporting make it difficult to detect and attribute equity gaps, justifying calls for gender-aware data systems, registry improvements, and transparent reporting standards. <cite id="50ae3102-1">Inadequate reporting of sex/gender in results and inconsistent terminology suggest that future systematic reviews require standardized, gender-aware data collection and reporting frameworks.</cite> <cite id="cdcb9664-2">Jurisdictions have not planned rigorous research to sustain pay equity policies’ ethical justification, implying a need for comparable administrative data and transparent evaluation protocols.</cite>

- Why mechanisms (beliefs, negotiation, mobility): evidence on U-shaped gaps and expectations suggests mechanisms like biased beliefs and negotiation styles contribute, calling for mechanism-focused, standardized causal designs. <cite id="99f6604d-2">Gender gaps appear at early career expectations and are pronounced at tails of the distribution; studies attribute parts of the gap to sorting and negotiation styles, motivating future mechanism-focused syntheses with causal identification.</cite>

# Which recommendation is most justified by the cited evidence gaps

- Most justified: rigorous causal identification (including quasi-experiments and policy natural experiments), standardized measurement, and intersectional decomposition, integrated into transparent, comparable data systems, and linked to policy evaluations.
  - Rationale: Multiple reviews explicitly flag that descriptive studies are insufficient for policy justification and that jurisdictions lack rigorous, comparable evaluations of pay equity policies; they also document pervasive gender-blindness and inconsistent measurement that mask heterogeneity and mechanisms. Together, these gaps directly justify a priority on causal identification, measurement standardization, and intersectional decomposition implemented via robust data infrastructure and transparent reporting, and then feeding into policy evaluations. <cite id="cdcb9664-2">Pay equity policies often lack rigorous ex ante/ex post justifications; jurisdictions have not planned the rigorous research needed, and the onus is on advocates to show benefits exceed harms, which motivates causal designs and systematic policy evaluation.</cite> <cite id="50ae3102-1">Gender-blind reporting and inconsistent terminology leave key equity dimensions under-studied, indicating that standardized, gender-aware data and transparent reporting are prerequisites for credible systematic reviews.</cite> <cite id="cdcb9664-1">Decomposition evidence shows that residuals reflect institutional structures (wage structures, segregation, returns), so future reviews must integrate intersectional, institutional breakdowns with causal designs.</cite> <cite id="fbc200a3-1">Cross-country variability in metrics underscores the need for standardized, comparable measurement as a foundation for synthesis and policy learning.</cite>
  - Trade-offs: Reviews also note that interventions can have unintended consequences, so systematic reviews must incorporate careful design and monitoring; this reinforces the causal-identification recommendation rather than displacing it. <cite id="99f6604d-0">Intervention reviews highlight both promise and unintended consequences, underscoring the need for rigorous, standardized evaluations with attention to side effects.</cite>

# Practical guidance for designing future systematic reviews

- Scope and questions: Pair a focused topic (e.g., within-firm wage discrimination in tech/finance; part-time to full-time transitions) with an explicit causal question and an intersectional scope (gender × race/ethnicity × disability). <cite id="cdcb9664-1">Residual gaps depend on institutional context (wage structures, segregation), so frameworks should stratify by sector, occupation, and institutional features.</cite>
- Inclusion criteria and measurement: Require harmonized definitions (wages vs earnings; job-to-job vs tenure; within vs between firm), report pay components (overtime/commission), and standardize decomposition metrics and controls. <cite id="cdcb9664-0">Decomposition studies show that national wage structures and returns drive observed gaps, motivating transparent, comparable decomposition protocols.</cite> <cite id="fbc200a3-1">Global monitoring demonstrates how differing bases (hourly wages vs median income) change estimates, necessitating harmonized definitions in inclusion criteria.</cite>
- Methods: Mandate quasi-experimental designs (IV, DiD, regression discontinuity, natural experiments in policy shocks) and registry linkage to administrative wage data; preregister analysis plans to address gender-blindness and reporting gaps. <cite id="cdcb9664-2">The lack of rigorous justification for pay equity policies, and the absence of planned rigorous research, argue for mandatory causal designs and transparent protocols in future reviews.</cite> <cite id="50ae3102-1">Low reporting of sex/gender in results argues for preregistered, gender-aware analysis plans and transparent reporting standards.</cite>
- Data infrastructure: Partner with labor statistics agencies and employers to access gender-disaggregated, job-level data; adopt common taxonomies for work arrangements and occupations; and publish codebooks and gender-blindness audits. <cite id="cdcb9664-2">No jurisdiction appears to contemplate the rigorous research infrastructure needed; building comparable, transparent data systems is a prerequisite for credible policy evaluation.</cite> <cite id="fbc200a3-2">International monitoring initiatives imply a role for standardized, comparable datasets across jurisdictions.</cite>
- Policy linkage: Pre-register effect decomposition (direct vs mediated via segregation, human capital, beliefs) and conduct cost-effectiveness and equity-impact analyses for each intervention; include negative/zero-result reporting to correct publication bias. <cite id="99f6604d-0">Intervention reviews show both benefits and unintended consequences, necessitating comprehensive, preregistered policy evaluations with transparent reporting of nulls.</cite> <cite id="50ae3102-1">Gendered impact assessments are less common than cost-effectiveness analyses; future reviews should balance both and report equity outcomes as routinely as effectiveness.</cite>

In sum, contemporary wage-gap reviews converge on a call for systematic reviews that are causally rigorous, intersectionally disaggregated, measurement-standardized, data-transparent, and tightly coupled to policy evaluation. Among these, the most justified immediate priority is to build causal-capable, intersectional, and standardized evidence pipelines (measurement + data infrastructure + methods + transparent reporting) because these directly address the evidence gaps that reviews themselves document—gender-blindness, inconsistent metrics, and the insufficiency of descriptive analyses for policy justification. <cite id="cdcb9664-2">Pay equity policies’ lack of rigorous justification and the absence of planned rigorous research underscore the centrality of causal-capable pipelines.</cite> <cite id="50ae3102-1">Gender-blindness and inconsistent terminology/reporting are foundational gaps requiring standardized, transparent frameworks.</cite> <cite id="cdcb9664-1">Residual gaps reflect institutional structures and segregation, motivating intersectional decomposition integrated with causal designs.</cite> <cite id="fbc200a3-1">Cross-country variability in metrics highlights the necessity of harmonized measurement and comparable data systems.</cite>

Below is a synthesis of what recent wage-gap review papers recommend for future systematic reviews, followed by which recommendation is most strongly justified by the evidence gaps they themselves identify.

# What review papers identify as high-priority topics for future systematic reviews

- Causal identification and quasi-experimental designs
  - Reviewers consistently call for studies that move beyond correlation to identify causal mechanisms behind pay gaps, emphasizing quasi-experiments, instrumental variables, and policy natural experiments to attribute effects to gendered practices, discrimination, or structural barriers rather than confounded differences in human capital or choice. <cite id="cdcb9664-2">With the exception of the European Union, no jurisdiction has contemplated the need for the sort of rigorous research that is necessary to sustain public support and ethical justification for pay equity policies; with the onus on advocates to show these policies do more good than harm, rigorous, causal analyses are highlighted as a gap and a priority for future research agendas. 
  - Reviews of interventions also urge systematic synthesis on the effectiveness and side effects of institutional remedies (e.g., bans on salary history questions, pay transparency) to clarify causal links between policy changes and pay equity outcomes. <cite id="99f6604d-0">A review of interventions to reduce gender gaps in negotiation outcomes assesses effectiveness in reducing the gender pay gap and flags unintended consequences that warrant caution, underscoring the need for more causal and policy-focused evaluations.</cite>

- Intersectionality and heterogeneity across identities and work arrangements
  - Meta-reviews and policy evidence syntheses stress that the “gender pay gap” masks large within-country heterogeneity across race/ethnicity, disability, part-time/contract work, sector, occupation, firm size, and institutional context. <cite id="cdcb9664-1">Comparative literature highlights that differences in industrial and occupational segregation, returns to characteristics, and national wage structures account for substantial cross-country variation; within countries, the residual gap often reflects unobserved structural and institutional conditions, motivating systematic analyses that stratify by identity and work arrangements.</cite> 
  - Reviews in related domains show that gender-blind research practices and poor reporting on sex/gender contribute to persistent evidence gaps on equity impacts, reinforcing the need for intersectional, disaggregated future syntheses. <cite id="50ae3102-1">A reanalysis finds that gendered impact assessments are substantially less common than cost-effectiveness analyses and documents inadequate reporting of sex/gender across methods and results, suggesting that intersectional, disaggregated reviews are needed to close these gaps.</cite>

- Measurement and definitions (wages vs earnings; job-to-job vs tenure; within vs between firm; overtime/commissions)
  - Evidence reviews repeatedly note that widely used statistics (e.g., gender pay gap ratios) vary in definitions and denominators (average hourly wages vs median income; full-time vs all workers), and that pay components such as overtime and commissions are inconsistently measured. <cite id="fbc200a3-1">Global monitoring bodies report global gender pay gaps using average hourly wages for 73 countries (16%), with alternative factor-weighted estimates (19%), while OECD data show median income gaps of about 13.5% with wide cross-country variation; these discrepancies by metric and coverage motivate standardized measurement protocols in future reviews.</cite>
  - Reviews of decomposition techniques and sectoral comparisons emphasize the need for consistent decomposition frameworks and clearer attribution of “within-firm” versus “between-firm/sectoral” drivers across institutional contexts. <cite id="cdcb9664-0">Decomposition-based reviews attribute inter-sector gender pay gap dynamics to national wage structures and cross-country differences in returns to characteristics, underscoring the need for standardized decomposition and measurement practices in future syntheses.</cite>

- Sectoral/occupational segregation and occupational mobility
  - Cross-country reviews highlight that segregation patterns and national wage structures shape observed gender pay gaps, calling for systematic comparisons of sectoral/occupational segregation, occupational mobility, and returns across institutions. <cite id="cdcb9664-1">Cross-country studies identify national wage structures and cross-country differences in industrial and occupational segregation and returns to these characteristics as determinants of the GPG, suggesting a need for systematic, comparative analyses of segregation and mobility.</cite>
  - Policy-oriented reviews recommend mapping segregation dynamics over time to link segregation to pay gap trajectories and to evaluate impacts of sector-specific policies. <cite id="fbc200a3-2">ILO’s initiative on the wage gap between men and women in Latin America brings 173 countries together to address SDG Target 8.5, reflecting a regional agenda to systematically analyze sectoral and institutional drivers; this implies prioritizing sectoral/occupational breakdowns and cross-jurisdictional comparisons in future reviews.</cite>

- Data systems, transparency, and gender-blindness in research infrastructure
  - Reviews diagnose that many studies are gender-blind by design, with inconsistent reporting of sex/gender across methods and results and inadequate terminology (sex vs gender), which obscures equity-relevant heterogeneity. <cite id="50ae3102-1">Meta-analyses show that while sex/gender is often mentioned in methods (51–83%), it is reported in results less than 30% of the time, and terminology is inconsistently used; these gaps justify recommendations for standardized, gender-aware data collection, reporting, and registries for future systematic reviews.</cite>
  - Policy evidence syntheses argue that jurisdictions lack rigorous, jurisdiction-specific impact evaluations of pay equity policies, pointing to the need for centralized, comparable administrative data and transparency regimes to support systematic synthesis. <cite id="cdcb9664-2">No jurisdiction appears to contemplate the need for rigorous research to sustain pay equity policies’ ethical justification; future research agendas should include building comparable data systems and transparent evaluation protocols.</cite>

- Mechanism-focused and expectation-driven research
  - Survey reviews of beliefs and expectations emphasize under-studied mechanisms (e.g., biased beliefs, negotiation styles) and call for systematic tests of how these mechanisms interact with human capital and institutional context. <cite id="99f6604d-2">Evidence shows a U-shaped gender pay gap across the wage distribution and documents gender gaps in expected starting and lifetime earnings; related studies attribute substantial gaps to sorting and negotiation styles, motivating future mechanism-focused syntheses on beliefs, negotiation, and career pathing.</cite>
  - Reviews of negotiation interventions urge standardized evaluation designs and attention to unintended consequences, pointing to the need for systematic reviews that combine lab/field evidence with administrative outcomes. <cite id="99f6604d-0">A review of negotiation interventions and institutional changes documents both promise and unintended consequences, recommending standardized, causal evaluation frameworks and transparent reporting in future systematic reviews.</cite>

- Global and regional coverage with attention to non-OECD and emerging-economy contexts
  - Cross-national reviews note that progress differs sharply across OECD vs non-OECD countries and across EU member states, calling for systematic reviews that expand geographic coverage and harmonize measurement. <cite id="fbc200a3-1">According to OECD data, the differential in median income is about 13.5% and improving in OECD countries, while for non-OECD countries it is around 15% and worsening; across the EU, the salary gap ranges from 1.3% (Luxembourg) to 22.3% (Latvia), indicating a strong need for systematic, geographically disaggregated evidence syntheses.</cite>

# How the cited evidence gaps motivate these recommendations

- Why causal identification: reviews highlight that policy debates demand ex ante/ex post justifications and that rigorous causal research is underdeveloped relative to descriptive assessments, with pay equity policies often justified by positive claims alone. <cite id="cdcb9664-2">The policy analytic approach reveals that pay equity policies struggle to meet standard criteria of justification; rigorous causal research has been uncommon, and the onus is on advocates to demonstrate benefits exceed harms, underscoring the need for causal designs and systematic policy evaluations.</cite>

- Why intersectionality and heterogeneity: decomposition and cross-country comparisons show that unexplained residuals reflect institutional structures (wage structures, segregation, returns), not just individual differences, motivating disaggregated, intersectional analyses and standardized reporting. <cite id="cdcb9664-1">Observed gaps persist after accounting for observable characteristics, and differences in wage structures, segregation, and returns across countries and institutions explain much of the variation, implying that future reviews must stratify by identity, sector, and occupation with consistent measurement.</cite> <cite id="50ae3102-1">Gender-blind reporting and terminology inconsistencies leave key equity dimensions under-studied, justifying intersectional, disaggregated future syntheses.</cite>

- Why measurement standardization: conflicting definitions and coverage yield widely varying gap magnitudes; reviews note the need for consistent metrics (wages vs earnings; job-to-job vs tenure; within vs between firm) and pay components. <cite id="fbc200a3-1">Global monitoring uses different bases (average hourly wages vs median income) and shows large cross-country variation; this motivates standardized, comparable metrics in future systematic reviews.</cite> <cite id="cdcb9664-0">Decomposition methods attribute sectoral differences to national wage structures and returns, reinforcing a need for transparent, comparable decomposition protocols.</cite>

- Why sectoral/occupational segregation: cross-country analyses attribute substantial gaps to segregation and institutional context, calling for systematic comparisons and policy-linked evaluations. <cite id="cdcb9664-1">National wage structures and segregation patterns drive gap magnitude; systematic reviews should compare these mechanisms across institutions and over time.</cite> <cite id="fbc200a3-2">International initiatives to monitor wage gaps imply a research agenda emphasizing sectoral/occupational breakdowns and cross-jurisdictional comparisons.</cite>

- Why data/registry and transparency: pervasive gender-blindness and inconsistent reporting make it difficult to detect and attribute equity gaps, justifying calls for gender-aware data systems, registry improvements, and transparent reporting standards. <cite id="50ae3102-1">Inadequate reporting of sex/gender in results and inconsistent terminology suggest that future systematic reviews require standardized, gender-aware data collection and reporting frameworks.</cite> <cite id="cdcb9664-2">Jurisdictions have not planned rigorous research to sustain pay equity policies’ ethical justification, implying a need for comparable administrative data and transparent evaluation protocols.</cite>

- Why mechanisms (beliefs, negotiation, mobility): evidence on U-shaped gaps and expectations suggests mechanisms like biased beliefs and negotiation styles contribute, calling for mechanism-focused, standardized causal designs. <cite id="99f6604d-2">Gender gaps appear at early career expectations and are pronounced at tails of the distribution; studies attribute parts of the gap to sorting and negotiation styles, motivating future mechanism-focused syntheses with causal identification.</cite>

# Which recommendation is most justified by the cited evidence gaps

- Most justified: rigorous causal identification (including quasi-experiments and policy natural experiments), standardized measurement, and intersectional decomposition, integrated into transparent, comparable data systems, and linked to policy evaluations.
  - Rationale: Multiple reviews explicitly flag that descriptive studies are insufficient for policy justification and that jurisdictions lack rigorous, comparable evaluations of pay equity policies; they also document pervasive gender-blindness and inconsistent measurement that mask heterogeneity and mechanisms. Together, these gaps directly justify a priority on causal identification, measurement standardization, and intersectional decomposition implemented via robust data infrastructure and transparent reporting, and then feeding into policy evaluations. <cite id="cdcb9664-2">Pay equity policies often lack rigorous ex ante/ex post justifications; jurisdictions have not planned the rigorous research needed, and the onus is on advocates to show benefits exceed harms, which motivates causal designs and systematic policy evaluation.</cite> <cite id="50ae3102-1">Gender-blind reporting and inconsistent terminology leave key equity dimensions under-studied, indicating that standardized, gender-aware data and transparent reporting are prerequisites for credible systematic reviews.</cite> <cite id="cdcb9664-1">Decomposition evidence shows that residuals reflect institutional structures (wage structures, segregation, returns), so future reviews must integrate intersectional, institutional breakdowns with causal designs.</cite> <cite id="fbc200a3-1">Cross-country variability in metrics underscores the need for standardized, comparable measurement as a foundation for synthesis and policy learning.</cite>
  - Trade-offs: Reviews also note that interventions can have unintended consequences, so systematic reviews must incorporate careful design and monitoring; this reinforces the causal-identification recommendation rather than displacing it. <cite id="99f6604d-0">Intervention reviews highlight both promise and unintended consequences, underscoring the need for rigorous, standardized evaluations with attention to side effects.</cite>

# Practical guidance for designing future systematic reviews

- Scope and questions: Pair a focused topic (e.g., within-firm wage discrimination in tech/finance; part-time to full-time transitions) with an explicit causal question and an intersectional scope (gender × race/ethnicity × disability). <cite id="cdcb9664-1">Residual gaps depend on institutional context (wage structures, segregation), so frameworks should stratify by sector, occupation, and institutional features.</cite>
- Inclusion criteria and measurement: Require harmonized definitions (wages vs earnings; job-to-job vs tenure; within vs between firm), report pay components (overtime/commission), and standardize decomposition metrics and controls. <cite id="cdcb9664-0">Decomposition studies show that national wage structures and returns drive observed gaps, motivating transparent, comparable decomposition protocols.</cite> <cite id="fbc200a3-1">Global monitoring demonstrates how differing bases (hourly wages vs median income) change estimates, necessitating harmonized definitions in inclusion criteria.</cite>
- Methods: Mandate quasi-experimental designs (IV, DiD, regression discontinuity, natural experiments in policy shocks) and registry linkage to administrative wage data; preregister analysis plans to address gender-blindness and reporting gaps. <cite id="cdcb9664-2">The lack of rigorous justification for pay equity policies, and the absence of planned rigorous research, argue for mandatory causal designs and transparent protocols in future reviews.</cite> <cite id="50ae3102-1">Low reporting of sex/gender in results argues for preregistered, gender-aware analysis plans and transparent reporting standards.</cite>
- Data infrastructure: Partner with labor statistics agencies and employers to access gender-disaggregated, job-level data; adopt common taxonomies for work arrangements and occupations; and publish codebooks and gender-blindness audits. <cite id="cdcb9664-2">No jurisdiction appears to contemplate the rigorous research infrastructure needed; building comparable, transparent data systems is a prerequisite for credible policy evaluation.</cite> <cite id="fbc200a3-2">International monitoring initiatives imply a role for standardized, comparable datasets across jurisdictions.</cite>
- Policy linkage: Pre-register effect decomposition (direct vs mediated via segregation, human capital, beliefs) and conduct cost-effectiveness and equity-impact analyses for each intervention; include negative/zero-result reporting to correct publication bias. <cite id="99f6604d-0">Intervention reviews show both benefits and unintended consequences, necessitating comprehensive, preregistered policy evaluations with transparent reporting of nulls.</cite> <cite id="50ae3102-1">Gendered impact assessments are less common than cost-effectiveness analyses; future reviews should balance both and report equity outcomes as routinely as effectiveness.</cite>

In sum, contemporary wage-gap reviews converge on a call for systematic reviews that are causally rigorous, intersectionally disaggregated, measurement-standardized, data-transparent, and tightly coupled to policy evaluation. Among these, the most justified immediate priority is to build causal-capable, intersectional, and standardized evidence pipelines (measurement + data infrastructure + methods + transparent reporting) because these directly address the evidence gaps that reviews themselves document—gender-blindness, inconsistent metrics, and the insufficiency of descriptive analyses for policy justification. <cite id="cdcb9664-2">Pay equity policies’ lack of rigorous justification and the absence of planned rigorous research underscore the centrality of causal-capable pipelines.</cite> <cite id="50ae3102-1">Gender-blindness and inconsistent terminology/reporting are foundational gaps requiring standardized, transparent frameworks.</cite> <cite id="cdcb9664-1">Residual gaps reflect institutional structures and segregation, motivating intersectional decomposition integrated with causal designs.</cite> <cite id="fbc200a3-1">Cross-country variability in metrics highlights the necessity of harmonized measurement and comparable data systems.</cite></answer>

Title: Gender Differences in Negotiation: Can Interventions Reduce the Gap?
Snippet: Gender differences in negotiation are seen as contributing to the persistent gender gaps in labor market outcomes. We review the literature on interventions aiming to mute differences in negotiation and assess their effectiveness in reducing the gender pay gap. We present research on initiatives that aspire to increase how often and how women negotiate, as well as institutional changes that ban negotiations, ban requests for employee salary history, and improve wage transparency. Along with exploring the effectiveness of these initiatives, we point to unintended consequences that warrant caution at implementation. The review makes clear that initial efforts to push women to negotiate more like men have shifted to alter instead the conditions of the negotiation. This shift results not only from wanting to consider policies that “fix the institutions” rather than “fixing the women,” but also from evidence that these interventions are more successful in securing pay equity. Title: Gender Bias in Justice Evaluations of Earnings: Evidence From Three Survey Experiments
Snippet: Previous studies in sociological justice research have found mixed results on the gender bias in justice evaluations of earnings. Some studies report a just gender pay gap favoring men; others do not find this gap. This study investigates the gender bias in justice evaluations by linking it to the inequality structure in which people are embedded. The empirical analyses are based on three factorial survey studies that consist of fictitious full-time employees with varying characteristics, including gender. One study was conducted with social sciences students, and two used population samples of German inhabitants. The results show that social sciences students revealed no gender bias in their evaluations. In the population surveys, both men and women showed a rating behavior favoring male employees. Respondents living in federal states with high actual gender pay gaps produced a larger bias favoring men. The findings indicate that actual inequalities between men and women influence the gender bias in justice evaluations.

Snippet: Many studies in this line of research document a U-shaped pattern of the gender pay gap along the conditional and unconditional distributions of earnings, meaning that the gender pay gap is particularly pronounced in the lower (sticky floor effect) and upper tail (glass ceiling effect) of wage distributions (Antonczyk et al. 2010;Christofides et al. 2013).
